opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the interesting thing about where we are right now is that capability is no longer the main question. If you look at what these models can do today, folding laundry, clearing a table, assembling boxes, you can get a robot to do a surprisingly wide range of tasks at least some of the time. The demos are real. But "some of the time" is the problem.

When you think about actually deploying a robot in someone's home or in a warehouse or a factory, the bar isn't "can it do the task." The bar is "can it do the task ninety-nine-point-something percent of the time, for hours on end, without a person babysitting it." If a robot succeeds eighty percent of the time, that sounds impressive in a research paper, but in practice it means that every fifth attempt someone has to walk over and fix something. At that point, the economics just don't work. You've basically hired a person to supervise a machine that's slower than the person would have been.

And reliability is hard in robotics in a way that's different from, say, language models. In language, if the model makes a mistake, you can regenerate, you can edit, the cost of an error is usually pretty low. In the physical world, errors compound. If the robot drops a shirt slightly wrong, the next state it's in is one it may never have seen in training, and now it's off-distribution, and things can spiral from there. You also can't just undo a broken glass.

So the way I think about it is that the field has kind of crossed the threshold of generality. We've shown that one model can do many things. The next frontier is taking that generality and pushing it into the regime of robustness, getting the long tail of failure cases down. That's going to require a lot more real-world data, much better ways of learning from the model's own experience and mistakes, things like reinforcement learning on top of these foundation models, and probably better ways of the model recognizing when it's failing and recovering on its own.

I'd actually argue that once you crack reliability, deployment follows pretty naturally, because the demand is enormous. People want these robots. The thing holding it back is that you can't yet trust them to just do the job.

r001.rationale: The response says robot demos are real and that tasks work “at least some of the time,” but does not explain that a polished recorded demo may come from retrying until a successful take.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we've gotten surprisingly good at demos and surprisingly bad at the thing that actually matters, which is doing the task every single time.

When I look at the models we're building now, the thing that strikes me is that the capability surface is enormous. You can show a robot a new object, give it a language instruction it's never seen, put it in a kitchen it hasn't been in, and a reasonable fraction of the time it does something sensible. Five or six years ago that would have been unthinkable. So the question people naturally ask is, why isn't this everywhere already? And the answer is that "a reasonable fraction of the time" is the problem.

In most of the software world, a model that works ninety percent of the time is incredibly useful. If a language model gives you a slightly wrong answer, you read it, you catch it, you ask again. The cost of a mistake is low and the human is in the loop. In robotics, the robot is acting on the physical world. If it drops the glass, the glass is broken. If it does the task nine times out of ten, then in a real deployment that tenth time is what everyone remembers, and it's what determines whether anyone trusts the system enough to leave it alone. So the bar isn't ninety percent. Depending on the application it's ninety-nine, or ninety-nine point nine, and every one of those nines is harder than the last.

And the reason reliability is the bottleneck rather than, say, raw capability, is that the failures aren't the kind you can fix with a demo. They're long-tail. The lighting is a bit different, the gripper is slightly worn, someone put the mug upside down. Each individual case is rare, but there are infinitely many of them, and the real world is very good at finding the ones you didn't think of. We've seen this with autonomous driving, where getting to something that works most of the time happened relatively quickly, and then closing the last gap took a decade and is still ongoing.

The other piece is that reliability is what unlocks the flywheel. The reason we don't have enormous robot datasets the way we have enormous text datasets is that robots aren't out there doing useful work and generating experience. To get them out there, they have to be reliable enough that a business is willing to deploy them. Once they're deployed, you get data from real operation, which improves the model, which improves reliability, which lets you deploy more. But you have to cross that threshold first, and right now that threshold is the thing standing between a very impressive research result and a product that actually changes how work gets done.

So when I say reliability is the bottleneck, I don't mean it as a boring engineering detail. I think it's actually the central research problem. How do you get a learned system that generalizes to behave consistently, and how do you know when it's about to fail so it can ask for help instead of just going for it. If we crack that, I think the rest of the capability story follows pretty quickly.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts impressive demos with inconsistent real-world performance, but does not say that a polished recorded demo may be produced by retrying until a successful take.

astra-6.text:
Because there’s a big gap between getting a robot to do something once and getting it to do it reliably enough that somebody can depend on it. You can have a really impressive demonstration, but if the robot needs a person to intervene every few minutes, it’s very hard to make that useful in practice.

And robotics makes that particularly challenging because you’re interacting with the physical world. Objects move, lighting changes, something slips out of the gripper. A task that looks like one action actually involves a whole sequence of decisions, and small errors can compound. So even if each individual step is pretty good, the probability of completing the entire task can still be disappointing.

I think the key is that reliability doesn’t mean the robot never makes a mistake. It means it can recognize that something went wrong, recover, and, when it needs to, ask for help. That’s what lets you go from a system that works in a demo to a system you can actually leave running.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts impressive demonstrations with dependable operation, but does not say the recorded demonstration may have been achieved by retrying until a successful take.

sol-6.1.text:
Because in robotics, it’s not enough for a model to do something impressive once. It has to work consistently across all the little variations that happen in the real world: the lighting changes, an object is in a slightly different position, somebody bumps into the robot. And when it makes a mistake, it needs to be able to recover.

Think about a task that takes a hundred steps. Even if each step succeeds 99 percent of the time, the probability of completing the whole task can be surprisingly low. So a robot can look very capable in a short demonstration and still need frequent human intervention when you try to use it all day.

That’s why reliability is such a bottleneck. We need to move from showing that a robot can perform a task to knowing that it will perform it consistently, and that it can recognize when it needs help. That’s what makes it useful outside the lab.
